title: Why Do My Ankles Roll In on Inline Speed Skates?
thumbnail_text: Ankles rolling in? It is rarely weak ankles

scenes.heading: Why Do My Ankles Roll In on Inline Speed Skates?
scenes.sub: Four causes to check before any strength work
scenes.narration: If your ankles roll in on inline speed skates, this guide shows you how to find the real cause and fix it. You will learn a two minute test you can do at home, the four usual causes, and the ankle work that helps. Here is the good news. The cause is usually not weak ankles. It is almost always one of four things. Your weight sits inside the wheel line. Your wheels have worn into a slope. Your frame is mounted off to one side. Or your boot is not holding your heel down. Three of those change the same afternoon you fix them.

scenes.heading: Rolling in is not the same as leaning
bullets: Skate tips in during the glide
One skate's wheels more coned
Arch aches, quads barely used
Kneecap sits inside the big toe
Constant small ankle corrections
scenes.narration: First, be clear about what you are fixing. Every stroke in speed skating puts the skate on an edge on purpose. That is not collapse. Collapse is when the skate tips inward while you are simply gliding, with no push, and you cannot stop it. Look for these signs. The skate tips in during the glide, not only the push. One skate's wheels are more coned than the other's. Your arch aches after a session while your quads feel barely used. Standing still, your kneecap sits inside the line of your big toe. If the skate only tips when you push hard, you are probably fine. Edge work is the sport.

scenes.heading: The two minute standing test
bullets: Lace up as normal, stand by a wall
Check kneecap against mid foot
Stand on one skate, watch the frame
Loosen the cuff and repeat
Repeat the single leg stand barefoot
scenes.narration: Before you buy anything or start any exercises, do this test on a flat floor at home. Put your skates on and lace them exactly as you normally would. Hold a wall lightly and note where your kneecap sits compared with the middle of your foot. Now let go and stand on one skate for a few seconds, then the other. Watch the frame, not your knee. Next, loosen the laces from the ankle upward and repeat. If the roll improves, the closure is forcing it. Finally, step out of the skates and do the same single leg stand barefoot. If your ankle rolls in barefoot too, your foot and ankle are part of the story. If your barefoot stance is quiet, the gear is doing it to you, and no amount of calf raises will fix that.

scenes.heading: Collapse is not a lean
scenes.narration: This diagram shows the difference from the front. On the left, the ankle has rolled in. The shin stays upright, but the boot and frame fold inward underneath it. The orange line shows the load landing to the inside of the contact patch, the only narrow strip of road you are standing on. On the right, the ankle is stacked. Shin, boot and wheel sit in one straight column, so the load lands right on the contact patch. In a proper lean, the whole column tips together. In a collapse, only the bottom of it folds.

scenes.heading: Cause one: weight inside the wheel line
bullets: The most common cause by far
Contact strip is only millimetres wide
Worst at low speed and long glides
Fix it from the hip, not the ankle
scenes.narration: The first cause is the most common by a long way, and it is a technique problem, not a gear problem. A single line of wheels gives you a contact strip only a few millimetres across. Your foot has to be parked right on top of it. When your hips sit even slightly to the inside, your ankle is left holding a sideways load it has almost no leverage against. It tires quickly and starts to fold. The giveaway is timing. The roll is worst at low speed and during long glides, and it almost disappears when you skate hard and change feet quickly. The correction belongs to the hip, not the ankle. You build it by holding low glides on one skate for far longer than feels useful.

scenes.heading: Cause two: wheels worn into a slope
bullets: Wheels wear from the loaded shoulder
A ramp tilts your skate on every load
Check the profile end on at eye level
Flip and swap skates when rotating
Replace all eight for matched profiles
scenes.narration: The second cause is easy to miss. Speed wheels do not wear flat. They wear from the shoulder you load, which for most skaters is the inner shoulder. As that shoulder goes, the crown moves off centre. The wheel stops offering a high point in the middle and starts offering a ramp, so your skate sits at a small angle every time you load it. Take a wheel off, hold it at eye level, and look at the profile end on. If the two shoulders are not mirror images, that wheel is tilting your foot. When you rotate, flip each wheel over and move it to the other skate. And if a set has coned badly, it is finished for stability training. Replacing all eight at once gives you matched profiles.

scenes.heading: Frame too far out
scenes.narration: The third cause is frame position. Your wheel line wants to sit directly under the point your foot actually loads. In this diagram, the orange dot is where your foot presses down. On the left, the frame is mounted too far to the outside, so the wheel line sits outboard of that point. Every bit of load you put through the skate becomes a small turning force that rolls the boot inward, for the whole session, with no technique fault at all. On the right, the frame sits right under the load, and the wheel line and the load line agree.

scenes.heading: Moving the frame and ride height
bullets: Mark the frame position in pencil
Move it inward about 2mm at a time
One skate at a time to compare
Go back a step if the arch complains
Taller wheels make small errors bigger
scenes.narration: Most speed boots allow a few millimetres of sideways adjustment at the mounting points, so this usually costs nothing. Mark the current position on the boot sole with a pencil before you loosen the bolts. Then move the frame toward the inside of the foot in steps of about two millimetres. If your arch starts complaining, go back a step, because a frame too far inside loads the arch on every stroke. Ride height matters too. A taller wheel lifts you further off the road, so the same small tilt at the ankle carries your weight further from the wheel line. If you are fighting stability on 110mm wheels, dropping to a 90mm or 100mm setup for a block of training is a smart move, not a step backward.

scenes.heading: Cause four: the boot is not holding your heel
bullets: Heel lift moves your foot every stroke
Pull laces hard over the instep
Ease off above the ankle bone
The cuff should still fold forward
scenes.narration: The fourth cause is the boot. If your heel lifts inside it, your foot slides a few millimetres on every stroke and lands somewhere slightly different each time. Your ankle spends the whole session hunting for a position it never gets to keep. Most skaters lace this the wrong way. They pull the top of the cuff as tight as they can. That restricts the forward ankle flex you need to get low, and it leaves the heel just as free. Instead, pull the laces hard over the instep, above the arch. That is the band that drives your heel back into the heel cup. Above the ankle bone, ease off. A cuff you can still fold forward with your hand will let you get low.

scenes.heading: Ankle and foot work that helps
bullets: Resisted inversion with a band
Short foot holds, ten seconds
Tibialis anterior raises
Slow calf raises, full range
Ten minutes, most days, six to eight weeks
scenes.narration: If the barefoot test showed a roll, strength work belongs in your week. Gear faults change the same afternoon. Strength changes over six to eight weeks of consistent, boring work. Ten minutes on most days is plenty. Start with resisted inversion. Anchor a band on the outside of your foot and turn the sole inward against it. This trains the muscle that holds your arch up. Next, short foot holds. Draw the ball of your foot gently back toward the heel so the arch domes, keep your toes relaxed, and hold for ten seconds. Add raises for the front of the shin. Then slow calf raises through the full range, two legs first, then one leg, controlled on the way down. None of it needs equipment. Consistency is the whole trick.

scenes.heading: When to get it looked at
bullets: Sharp pain or visible swelling
Numbness or tingling in the foot
An ankle that gives way
Pain lasting days after skating
A previously sprained ankle
scenes.narration: Everything in this guide is general training advice, not a diagnosis. See a physiotherapist or a doctor rather than working through it yourself if you have sharp pain in or around the ankle, visible swelling, numbness or tingling in the foot, or an ankle that gives way under you. The same goes for any pain that lasts more than a few days after you stop skating. And if your ankle has been sprained before, get professional advice on loading it. The ligaments and balance reflexes both need specific work after an injury, and a general list will not cover it.

scenes.heading: Check the gear before you blame the ankle
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: So here is where to start. Do the two minute standing test tonight. If the roll disappears barefoot, check your wheel profiles and your frame position before you look at yourself. If it is there barefoot as well, start the ankle work and give it two months, while watching for the warning signs. Either way, hold more single leg glides than feels comfortable. A skater who can stand quietly on one skate at low speed has already solved most of this. The full guide, with the answers on ankle support and insoles, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
